questions.q: What happened to the US prison population from the 1970s to today?
a: It grew from about 300,000 to 2.3 million
It fell from about 2 million to 500,000
It stayed close to 300,000 the whole time
It doubled from 1 million to 2 million
questions.why: Lesson 1 gives those figures to show the scale of mass incarceration.

questions.q: What was the woman in the summary's example imprisoned for?
a: Writing bad checks to pay for her children's Christmas gifts
Stealing food from a local grocery store
Driving without a valid license
Failing to pay a parking ticket
questions.why: Lesson 1 says each check was under 150 dollars, yet she received a long sentence.

questions.q: How does the lifetime imprisonment rate for African Americans compare with the general population?
a: One in three, versus one in fifteen overall
One in ten, versus one in fifty overall
One in two, versus one in twenty overall
One in five, versus one in ten overall
questions.why: Lesson 2 contrasts the one-in-three rate with the one-in-fifteen national figure.

questions.q: What does the summary say about children in the justice system?
a: Some as young as 13 were jailed and tried as adults
All minors were moved into counseling programs
Children could not be sentenced before 2005
Only teenagers over 16 faced adult courts
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes minors tried and punished as adults, with no minimum age in Florida.

questions.q: What did the case of Walter McMillan show about prison's reach?
a: A conviction affects family and community, not just the prisoner
Death row inmates rarely receive any visitors
Small towns recover quickly from highly public trials
Wrongful convictions are usually overturned quickly
questions.why: Lesson 3 says more than 30 family members were affected by his conviction.
